1.title: The Best of Fukuoka in 24 Hours

periods.title: Ohori Park & Fukuoka Castle Ruins
periods.text: Start with a morning walk around Ohori Park, a beautiful lake park modeled after West Lake in Hangzhou, with a jogging path, traditional Japanese garden (¥250), and coffee kiosks. Walk to the adjacent Fukuoka Castle ruins (free) in Maizuru Park. The stone walls offer panoramic views of the city and bay. In cherry blossom season (late March–early April), the castle grounds are Fukuoka's prime hanami (flower-viewing) spot.
periods.tip: Ohori Park's Japanese garden is a hidden gem, a fraction of the cost of Kyoto gardens with the same meticulous beauty. Open 9am–5pm.

periods.title: Hakata Old Town & Canal City
periods.text: Walk through Hakata's old town. The Kushida Shrine (free) has been Hakata's spiritual centre for over 1,000 years and houses a stunning Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival float year-round. Explore the Kawabata Shotengai covered arcade, Fukuoka's oldest shopping street with traditional crafts and street snacks. Walk to Canal City Hakata, a massive shopping complex built around an artificial canal with a free fountain show every 30 minutes.
periods.tip: Kushida Shrine's permanent yamakasa float is 13 metres tall and elaborately decorated, one of the best free sights in Fukuoka.

periods.title: Yatai Street Stalls: Ramen & More
periods.text: Fukuoka's yatai (open-air food stalls) are legendary. Over 100 mobile stalls pop up at dusk along the Naka River and Tenjin area. Pull up a stool at a tiny counter (6–8 seats each) and order Hakata-style tonkotsu ramen (¥700–900): milky pork bone broth, thin straight noodles, and chashu pork. Order kae-dama (extra noodles, ¥100–150) when your bowl is half-empty. Try multiple yatai. Each has its own recipe.
periods.tip: Yatai along the Naka River near Nakasu island are the most atmospheric. Stalls open around 6pm and run until 2am. Cash only.

periods.title: Kushida Shrine & Hakata Machiya Museum
periods.text: Start at Kushida Shrine (free), Hakata's most important shrine for over 1,200 years. The elaborate yamakasa festival float on permanent display stands 13 metres tall and is lavishly decorated. Walk to the Hakata Machiya Folk Museum (¥200), a beautifully restored traditional merchant house showcasing Hakata's crafts including weaving and pottery. The surrounding old town streets feel pleasantly unhurried.
periods.tip: The Hakata Machiya museum demonstrates live Hakata-ori textile weaving. The artisans are friendly and will explain the process.

periods.title: Kawabata Arcade & Yanagibashi Market
periods.text: Walk the Kawabata Shotengai covered arcade, Fukuoka's oldest shopping street with traditional shops, manga cafes, and snack stands. Try mentaiko (spicy cod roe, ¥200–400 per piece), Fukuoka's signature ingredient. Continue to Yanagibashi Market, a compact, authentic market where locals buy fish, vegetables, and pickles. Lunch at one of the market restaurants: chirashi-don (scattered sushi, ¥800–1,200) with fish cut minutes earlier.
periods.tip: Yanagibashi Market is Fukuoka's real food market: no tourists, just locals. The sashimi here is fresher and cheaper than any restaurant.

periods.title: Nakasu Yatai & River Walk
periods.text: The yatai along the Naka River near Nakasu Island are Fukuoka at its most magical. These tiny mobile food stalls seat 6–8 people each and serve Hakata tonkotsu ramen (¥700–900), gyoza, yakitori, and oden. The atmosphere (sitting by the river, steam rising, strangers becoming friends over beer) is uniquely Fukuoka. Try 2–3 different yatai. Afterwards, walk along the illuminated Naka River.
periods.tip: Arrive at yatai between 7–8pm for shorter waits. Don't linger too long. Other customers are waiting. Eat, drink, move to the next.

periods.title: Ohori Park & Castle Ruins
periods.text: Morning walk around Ohori Park. The lake, bridges, and reflections are serene. The Japanese Garden (¥250) inside the park is a miniature masterpiece of traditional landscaping. Walk to Fukuoka Castle ruins in Maizuru Park (free). The stone walls and elevated grounds offer city and bay views. The castle was once Kyushu's largest, and the scale of the remaining stonework is impressive.
periods.tip: The castle ruins' highest point offers 360-degree views. In spring, 1,000+ cherry trees make this Fukuoka's hanami headquarters.

periods.title: Dazaifu Tenmangu Day Trip
periods.text: Train from Tenjin to Dazaifu (Nishitetsu line, ¥410, 40 minutes). Dazaifu Tenmangu is one of Japan's most important Shinto shrines, dedicated to the god of learning. The approach street is lined with mochi shops. The famous umegae mochi (plum-stamped rice cake, ¥130) has been sold here for centuries. The shrine grounds include plum gardens, koi ponds, and the Kyushu National Museum (¥700) nearby.
periods.tip: Dazaifu's Starbucks, designed by Kengo Kuma with interlocking wooden beams, is architecturally famous. Worth a photo even if you skip the coffee.

periods.title: Tenjin Underground & Izakaya Night
periods.text: Tenjin is Fukuoka's main shopping and entertainment district. The Tenjin Underground City stretches 590 metres with shops and restaurants. For dinner, find a local izakaya in the Tenjin backstreets. Order motsu nabe (tripe hot pot, ¥1,200–1,500 per person), Fukuoka's other signature dish. Rich, garlicky miso broth with beef intestines, cabbage, and chili flakes. Pair with shochu (Kyushu's native spirit, ¥400–600).
periods.tip: Motsu nabe is a must-try Fukuoka dish most tourists miss. Ooyama in Tenjin is the most famous. Expect a queue after 7pm.

periods.title: Momochi Beach & Fukuoka Tower
periods.text: Metro to Momochi for Fukuoka's urban beach, a man-made but pleasant sandy stretch with views across Hakata Bay. Walk to Fukuoka Tower (¥800). At 234 metres, it's Japan's tallest seaside tower with panoramic views of the city, mountains, and ocean. The surrounding Momochi district is modern and spacious, a contrast to the compact old town. The Fukuoka City Museum (¥200) nearby has the famous gold seal given by a Chinese emperor in 57 AD.
periods.tip: Fukuoka Tower has a lovers' spot on the observation deck, but the views are equally romantic for solo travellers and friends.

periods.title: Hakata Station & Deitos Shopping
periods.text: Hakata Station's shopping complex (Hakata Deitos, Amu Plaza) has excellent souvenir shopping: mentaiko in decorative boxes (¥1,000–3,000), Hakata-ori textiles, Chidori manju sweet cakes, and region-exclusive Kit Kat flavours. The rooftop garden (free) has a miniature shrine and city views. For a final ramen, Shin-Shin near Tenjin serves an excellent tonkotsu with a slightly lighter broth than the heavy Nagahama style.
periods.tip: Hakata Deitos has a "ramen stadium" on the 10th floor of Amu Plaza: eight ramen shops under one roof for comparison tasting.

periods.title: Final Yatai & Farewell
periods.text: One last evening at the yatai. Try the stalls along Watanabe-dori in Tenjin for a different selection from the Nakasu river stalls. Order ramen, gyoza, and a cold Asahi for the quintessential Fukuoka farewell. Hakata is the kind of city that quietly wins you over: the food, the warmth of the people, the easy pace. You'll already be planning your return before you've finished your last bowl.
periods.tip: Fukuoka Airport is incredibly close to the city: 5 minutes by metro from Hakata Station. No need to rush your final evening.

periods.title: Kushida Shrine & Old Town
periods.text: Start at Kushida Shrine (free), Hakata's spiritual centre for 1,200 years. The yamakasa festival float on display is 13 metres of elaborate decoration. Walk to the Hakata Machiya Folk Museum (¥200) for live textile weaving demonstrations. The surrounding old town has narrow lanes with traditional shophouses and a distinctly unhurried pace.
periods.tip: The Hakata Machiya museum demonstrates live Hakata-ori weaving. Artisans are friendly and explain the centuries-old process.

periods.title: Kawabata & Yanagibashi Market
periods.text: Walk Kawabata Shotengai arcade for traditional crafts and mentaiko shops. Continue to Yanagibashi Market for ultra-fresh sashimi and local pickles. Lunch at a market restaurant: chirashi-don with fish cut minutes ago (¥800–1,200). The market is small but authentic. This is where Fukuoka's chefs buy their ingredients.
periods.tip: Yanagibashi Market is Fukuoka's real food market: no tourists, just locals. Sashimi is fresher and cheaper than any restaurant.

periods.title: Nakasu Yatai Night
periods.text: The yatai along the Naka River are Fukuoka's soul. Tiny mobile stalls seat 6–8 people: Hakata tonkotsu ramen (¥700–900), gyoza, yakitori, and oden. The atmosphere of river, steam, and strangers is unique. Try 2–3 different stalls. Each yatai owner has their own recipe, their own personality, and their own regulars. This is street food at its finest.
periods.tip: Arrive 7–8pm for shorter waits. Don't linger: eat, drink, move. Cash only. The river stalls are more atmospheric than Tenjin ones.

periods.title: Ohori Park & Japanese Garden
periods.text: Morning walk around Ohori Park. The lake and bridges are serene. The Japanese Garden (¥250) is a miniature masterpiece. Walk to Fukuoka Castle ruins (free) for city and bay views from the elevated stone walls. In spring, 1,000+ cherry trees bloom here. The park is where Fukuoka jogs, picnics, and relaxes. Join the morning rhythm.
periods.tip: The castle ruins' highest point offers 360-degree views. Bring a coffee from the park kiosk and enjoy the panorama.

periods.title: Dazaifu Tenmangu
periods.text: Train to Dazaifu (Nishitetsu, ¥410, 40 min). Dazaifu Tenmangu shrine is dedicated to learning. The approach street sells umegae mochi (¥130) made on the spot. The shrine has plum gardens, koi ponds, and an atmosphere of studious devotion. Kengo Kuma's Starbucks with its stunning wooden lattice is worth photographing. The Kyushu National Museum (¥700) nearby is excellent.
periods.tip: Dazaifu's Kengo Kuma Starbucks is architecturally famous. The interlocking wooden beams are stunning. Photo-worthy even without coffee.

periods.title: Motsu Nabe & Tenjin Night
periods.text: Dinner is motsu nabe, Fukuoka's other signature dish. Rich miso broth with beef intestines, cabbage, garlic, and chili (¥1,200–1,500 per person). Ooyama in Tenjin is the most famous spot. Pair with Kyushu shochu, the local spirit, often made from sweet potato or barley. Walk the Tenjin backstreets for bars and the Tenjin Underground shopping city.
periods.tip: Motsu nabe at Ooyama is best reserved. Call ahead or queue from 5pm. Their miso-based broth is the definitive version.

periods.title: Nagasaki Peace Park & Atomic Bomb Museum
periods.text: Shinkansen or Kamome Express to Nagasaki (2 hours from Hakata). The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum (¥200) is devastating and essential: artifacts, survivor testimonies, and a meticulous timeline of August 9, 1945. The Peace Park and its iconic statue are nearby. The Hypocenter Park marks the exact point of detonation. The experience is sobering and profoundly moving.
periods.tip: Allow 2 hours minimum for the museum. The English audio guide adds crucial context. Bring tissues. The survivor accounts are heartbreaking.

periods.title: Glover Garden & Chinatown
periods.text: Walk through Nagasaki's Dutch Slopes and Glover Garden (¥620), a hilltop garden with Western-style mansions from the 1860s when Nagasaki was Japan's only port open to foreign trade. Views across the harbour are stunning. Lunch in Nagasaki Chinatown (the oldest in Japan) for champon (thick noodle soup with seafood and vegetables, ¥800–1,200), Nagasaki's signature dish. The pork buns (kakuni manju, ¥400) are also exceptional.
periods.tip: Glover Garden's Puccini connection: Madame Butterfly was set here, and the views explain why. The sunset from the garden is unforgettable.

periods.title: Mount Inasa Night View & Return
periods.text: If time allows, ride the ropeway to Mount Inasa (¥1,250 round trip) for Nagasaki's famous night view, rated one of Japan's top three alongside Hakodate and Kobe. The harbour lights reflecting on the water create a stunning panorama. Return to Fukuoka on the last train. If short on time, catch an earlier train and end the evening at Fukuoka's yatai stalls.
periods.tip: Mount Inasa night view is best after dark. The ropeway runs until 10pm. Check the last train back to Fukuoka before going up.

periods.title: Nokonoshima Island
periods.text: Ferry from Meinohama port to Nokonoshima Island (¥230, 10 minutes). This small island in Hakata Bay has flower gardens (¥1,200), hiking trails, beaches, and a tiny village with a pottery workshop. The Island Park has seasonal flowers: cosmos in autumn, rapeseed in spring, sunflowers in summer. The pace here is island-slow, with panoramic city views across the water.
periods.tip: Nokonoshima is best in spring (rapeseed) or autumn (cosmos). The island has a few restaurants but bringing a picnic adds to the experience.

periods.title: Momochi Beach & Tower
periods.text: Return and head to Momochi Beach, Fukuoka's urban beach with Hakata Bay views. Walk to Fukuoka Tower (¥800) for panoramic views from 234 metres. The city, mountains, and ocean stretch in every direction. The Fukuoka City Museum (¥200) displays the famous gold seal given by Chinese Emperor Guangwu in 57 AD, one of Japan's most important archaeological artifacts.
periods.tip: Fukuoka Tower's sunset views are the best in the city. Time your visit for 30 minutes before golden hour.

periods.title: Nagahama Ramen District
periods.text: Nagahama, near the fish market, is the birthplace of Hakata's tonkotsu ramen style. The ramen here is the most hardcore version: ultra-rich, ultra-porky broth with thin, hard noodles. Shin Shin and Nagahama Number One are the legendary shops (¥600–800). The area is rough around the edges but authentically Hakata. Order barikata (extra-firm) noodles and kae-dama (refill, ¥100) like a local.
periods.tip: Nagahama ramen shops are tiny and fast. You'll be in and out in 15 minutes. That's the culture. Order at the vending machine, sit, eat, leave.

periods.title: Beppu: Hell Tour
periods.text: Limited express train from Hakata to Beppu (¥5,250 or JR Pass, 2 hours). Beppu is Japan's most famous hot spring city with more thermal water output than anywhere except Yellowstone. Start with the "Hells Tour" (Jigoku Meguri, ¥2,200 combined ticket), seven dramatically colored hot springs including blood-red Chinoike Jigoku, cobalt-blue Umi Jigoku, and the boiling mud of Oniishibozu.
periods.tip: Buy the combined ¥2,200 ticket for all seven hells. Individual tickets cost ¥450 each. Umi Jigoku and Chinoike Jigoku are the most impressive.

periods.title: Sand Bath & Onsen
periods.text: Try the famous sand bath at Beppu Beach Sand Bath (¥1,510). Attendants bury you in naturally heated black sand near the ocean. It's surreal, toasty, and deeply relaxing. Then soak in one of Beppu's hundreds of public onsen. Takegawara Onsen (¥300) is the most atmospheric, a wooden bathhouse dating to 1879 with sand baths in the basement. The mineral-rich water leaves your skin silky smooth.
periods.tip: Takegawara Onsen is Beppu's most historic bathhouse. The wooden building and steamy interior are unforgettable. Bring your own towel.

periods.title: Return & Fukuoka Night
periods.text: Train back to Fukuoka. For a change from ramen, try Fukuoka's excellent Korean food in Tenjin. The city has a large Korean community and restaurants serving authentic bibimbap, tteokbokki, and Korean BBQ at prices rivaling Seoul. Or visit the Tenjin yatai stalls you haven't tried yet. Every stall owner has their own specialities: tempura yatai, oden yatai, and even French-influenced yatai exist.
periods.tip: Fukuoka's proximity to Korea means the Korean food here is genuinely excellent. The Tenjin area has the best concentration.

periods.title: Tocho-ji Temple & Hakata Crafts
periods.text: Visit Tocho-ji temple (free) for the Great Buddha of Hakata, a 10.8-metre seated wooden Buddha that's Kyushu's largest. The adjacent five-story pagoda is beautiful. Walk through the old Hakata craft district. The area around Reisen Park has pottery workshops and Hakata doll (Hakata ningyo) studios where you can watch artisans paint the famous clay figurines. Some offer ¥1,000–3,000 painting experiences.
periods.tip: Hakata ningyo dolls are a traditional souvenir: handpainted clay figures of samurai, geisha, and children. Studios offer painting workshops.

periods.title: Mentaiko Factory & Tasting
periods.text: Visit the Fukuya mentaiko factory or shop in Nakasu. Fukuya invented mentaiko (spicy marinated cod roe) in 1949. Free tastings of different spice levels. Buy mentaiko to take home (vacuum-packed, ¥800–2,000). Then walk to the Hakata Riverain Mall for lunch. The area has excellent curry rice and katsu restaurants. The Fukuoka Asian Art Museum (¥200) in the same building has rotating Asian contemporary art.
periods.tip: Fukuya is the original mentaiko company. Their Nakasu main shop offers generous free tastings. The "original hot" flavour is the classic.

periods.title: Yakitori Alley & Local Nightlife
periods.text: Fukuoka's yakitori (grilled chicken skewers) scene is underrated. Head to the small restaurants around Hakata Station's south side. Each specializes in different cuts. Chicken skin (kawa), heart (hatsu), and tsukune (meatball) skewers cost ¥100–200 each. Pair with highballs (¥300–400). The intimate atmosphere of these tiny shops (charcoal smoke, counter seating, and friendly chefs) is quintessential Japanese hospitality.
periods.tip: Fukuoka yakitori joints near Hakata Station south exit are cash-only and seat 10–15 people. Go early (6pm) or face a queue.

periods.title: Morning Onsen & Slow Start
periods.text: Start your final day at a sento (public bath). Nami Kaze no Yu near Momochi offers ocean views from its baths (¥800). Or try Manyo Club in Canal City (¥2,000) for a full onsen experience with city views. The morning soak ritual is deeply Japanese. Let the hot water prepare you for the day. Breakfast at a local kissaten (coffee shop) for thick toast, hard-boiled eggs, and drip coffee (¥500–800 for a set).
periods.tip: Japanese kissaten (old-school coffee shops) serve "morning sets": coffee plus toast and egg for ¥500–800. The pace is intentionally slow.

periods.title: Final Shopping & Souvenirs
periods.text: Hakata Station's Deitos shopping complex is the best souvenir spot: mentaiko, Hakata Torimon (custard-filled buns, ¥1,000 for 8), Chidori Manju, and regional Kit Kats. For Hakata crafts, Kawabata arcade has traditional textiles and pottery. The Amu Plaza rooftop garden (free) offers a final city view. Tax-free shopping applies for purchases over ¥5,000 at department stores.
periods.tip: Hakata Torimon is Fukuoka's most-gifted souvenir, a soft bun filled with milky custard. Every local recommends them. Buy at the station.

periods.title: One Last Ramen
periods.text: Your farewell meal in Fukuoka can only be ramen. Return to your favourite yatai or try one you missed. Or go to Ichiran's headquarters in Hakata (their global fame started here) for their unique solo-booth dining experience: you order via sheet, the chef slides the bowl through a bamboo curtain, and you eat in focused, meditative silence. Fukuoka is a city that feeds your soul through your stomach.
periods.tip: Fukuoka Airport is 5 minutes by subway from Hakata Station, the closest major airport to a city centre in Japan. No need to rush.

budgetTips.title: Ramen capital
budgetTips.text: Fukuoka ramen is the cheapest in Japan: ¥600–900 per bowl at yatai and restaurants. Kae-dama (noodle refill) is ¥100–150. A full ramen dinner with beer runs under ¥1,500.

budgetTips.title: City transit
budgetTips.text: Fukuoka City Subway 1-day pass (¥640) covers all three lines. Individual rides ¥210–360. Walking between Hakata, Tenjin, and Nakasu takes 15–20 minutes, often faster than metro.

budgetTips.title: Free attractions
budgetTips.text: Kushida Shrine, Ohori Park, Fukuoka Castle ruins, Kawabata arcade, Tocho-ji temple, and the Naka River walk are all free. Yatai browsing is free entertainment until you sit down.

budgetTips.title: Airport proximity
budgetTips.text: Fukuoka Airport is 5 minutes from Hakata Station by subway (¥260). This saves a hotel night. You can sightsee until late and still catch an early flight.

budgetTips.title: Day trip savings
budgetTips.text: Dazaifu is only ¥410 by Nishitetsu train from Tenjin (40 min). Nagasaki and Beppu are 2 hours by train, perfect day trips without hotel changes.

budgetTips.title: Conbini strategy
budgetTips.text: Lawson and FamilyMart in Fukuoka have excellent mentaiko onigiri (¥150–200) and local bento (¥400–600). Quality rivals restaurant food at a fraction of the price.

budgetBreakdown.notes: Ramen & conbini → izakaya & motsu nabe → fine dining
Walking & day pass → IC card → taxi
Free shrines & parks → museums & tower → day trips
Conbini beer → yatai & izakaya → shochu bars

practicalInfo.title: Getting Around
items: Fukuoka City Subway has 3 lines: Airport Line connects the airport to Hakata and Tenjin in 5–11 minutes. Get an ICOCA or Suica card
The city is very walkable: Hakata, Nakasu, and Tenjin are within 20 minutes of each other on foot along the river
Nishitetsu buses supplement the subway. For day trips, JR trains from Hakata Station connect to Nagasaki, Beppu, and Kumamoto

practicalInfo.title: Connectivity
items: Fukuoka Airport has pocket WiFi rental counters (¥500–900/day). eSIMs from Ubigi or Airalo work well
Free WiFi at Fukuoka City WiFi hotspots: register once and connect at subway stations, tourist spots, and some cafes
Google Maps is highly accurate for Fukuoka transit. Download offline maps as backup for areas with weak signal

practicalInfo.title: Money
items: Cash is essential for yatai (all cash-only), many small restaurants, and markets. Carry ¥10,000+ in cash at all times
7-Eleven and Japan Post ATMs accept foreign cards. Larger restaurants and shops accept cards
No tipping in Japan. Yatai stall owners are grateful for a simple "gochisousama deshita" (thank you for the meal) when leaving

practicalInfo.title: Getting to Fukuoka
items: Fukuoka Airport (FUK) is Japan's most city-convenient airport: 5 minutes by subway to Hakata Station (¥260)
Shinkansen from Tokyo: 5 hours (¥22,220). From Osaka: 2.5 hours (¥15,280). JR Pass covers these routes
Ferries to Busan, South Korea depart from Hakata Port (from ¥9,000 one-way, 3 hours by jetfoil)

practicalInfo.title: Health & Safety
items: Fukuoka is very safe with negligible crime. The Nakasu entertainment district has some touts at night. Just walk past
No vaccinations required. Tap water is safe. Pharmacies (drugstores) are in every shopping area
Summer (Jul–Aug) is hot and humid (33°C+). Typhoon season (Aug–Oct) can disrupt transport. Check forecasts

practicalInfo.title: Packing Tips
items: Comfortable walking shoes: Fukuoka is flat and walkable. Slip-on shoes for temple visits
A small towel (tenugui): Japanese restrooms rarely have paper towels. Useful at yatai for wiping ramen splashes too
Rain gear for Fukuoka's rainy season (Jun–Jul). A light jacket for air-conditioned interiors in summer

culturalTips.title: Ramen Etiquette
culturalTips.text: Slurp loudly. It cools the noodles and shows appreciation. Eat fast. Hakata ramen is designed to be consumed quickly. Order kae-dama (noodle refill) while broth remains. Finish the broth if you loved it.

culturalTips.title: Yatai Culture
culturalTips.text: Yatai are communal. You sit next to strangers and conversation flows naturally. Don't hog seats during busy times. Order within 5 minutes of sitting. Cash only. Say "gochisousama" when leaving.

culturalTips.title: Shochu Culture
culturalTips.text: Kyushu drinks shochu, not sake. Made from sweet potato (imo), barley (mugi), or rice (kome). Ask for it mixed with hot water (oyuwari) or on the rocks (rokku). It's smoother than you expect.

culturalTips.title: Shoes & Manners
culturalTips.text: Remove shoes at temples, traditional restaurants, and ryokans. Slippers provided. Never wear toilet slippers outside the bathroom. Carry clean socks. Bare feet in shared spaces are awkward.

culturalTips.title: Hakata Dialect
culturalTips.text: Fukuoka people speak Hakata-ben dialect: "yokatai" (it's good), "bai" (ending particle), and "nantai" (what's that). Locals are proud of their dialect and warmer/friendlier than Tokyo stereotypes.

culturalTips.title: Festival Spirit
culturalTips.text: Hakata Gion Yamakasa (July 1–15) is the city's biggest festival: massive floats raced through the streets at dawn. Dontaku Festival (May 3–4) features 30,000 performers. If visiting during either, expect a wild time.
